subject: Mulitple helicopters cause detection function woes

messages.author: b5bdc2339bd092ab
messages.subject: Mulitple helicopters cause detection function woes
parts:
Hi,
 
I am looking for some guidance on what (if anything) Distance folks think could be done with some messy data I have.
 
We flew an aerial moose survey. Due to a variety of reasons beyond our control, we had to use 3 different helicopters over the course of the survey. This resulted in detection functions that look very different depending on the model of the helicopter (see attached). In particular one has very bad behavior near 0. Another issue is that each helicopter model was only used for a day or two, and so only sampled part of the survey area (see attached map). We do have some data from an adjoining study area that was also surveyed around the same time. Could this possibly be used to help fit the detection function? What other analysis options do I have?
 
Any advice would be appreciated. Even if it is a stern: "Do not analyze this mess!".
 
Of note, the first three days were done using EC-120/EC-130 helicopters and the last day was done using a Jet Ranger. The Jet Ranger is what we have used with success in the past. The results of this survey suggest that it is also what we stick with going forward!
 
Thanks,
Hannah

messages.subject: Re: Mulitple helicopters cause detection function woes
parts:
Hi,
 
I wanted to post about what I decided to do with the above data in case it is helpful to others.
 
Based on some feedback from Eric, it seems the histograms weren't as poorly behaved as I had though.
 
The key point was deciding if we had an issue with g(0)<1, as if not, then based on the property of pooling robustness, we could ignore variability in detectability by aircraft type, as we were just going for a density estimate for the whole survey (aircraft isn't really an interesting covariate, as sex or species might be).
 
We did decide to assume g(0)=1 after discussing more with the biologists regarding the visibility issues in the EC-120 in particular. It seems like the vision of the front observer (who is responsible for the area under the helicopter) was reduced only on the right from about 30-100 m from the line. Given that transects are not all flown in the same direction, and that the height of the aircraft varies during the survey, we decided that although some of the animals may have been missed in that region, visibiilty of the line itself (<30m) was good, and the g(0)=1 assumption was probably no more compromised than in a usual survey (due to canopy cover).
 
After right-truncation and selecting the best model (half-normal + cosine), I did try that model and include aircraft as a covariate. It was not supported by AIC, and so our final estimate is based on the half-normal + cosine.
 
I should also add that I was sorely tempted to try left-truncation to remove what I perceived as a hole at 0, but was saved from that by Eric's reminder that the final density estimate will likely be very sensitive to you choice of left-truncation distance, and in the absence of any independant information about the appropriate truncation distance, this is likely not a wise approach.
 
Hannah
